problems.html: (a) ∫x e2x  dx\displaystyle\int x\,\mathrm{e}^{2x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xe2xdx, (b) ∫xln⁡x  dx\displaystyle\int x\ln x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫xlnxdx.
hints: In both parts use LIATE to choose uuu: the factor that comes first in the list (logarithm, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential) is the one to differentiate.
In (a) that makes u=xu=xu=x and v′=e2xv'=\mathrm{e}^{2x}v′=e2x; in (b) the logarithm comes first, so u=ln⁡xu=\ln xu=lnx and v′=xv'=xv′=x.

Watch the constants. In (a) the 12\tfrac1221​ from integrating e2x\mathrm{e}^{2x}e2x appears twice; in (b) the leftover integrand 12x2⋅1x\tfrac12x^2\cdot\tfrac1x21​x2⋅x1​ simplifies to 12x\tfrac12x21​x.
problems.format: (a) at x=0, (b) at x=1; C=0; comma-separated

problems.html: ∫3x+1x(x+1)  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{3x+1}{x(x+1)}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x(x+1)3x+1​dx.
hints: Split into Ax+Bx+1\dfrac{A}{x}+\dfrac{B}{x+1}xA​+x+1B​ and clear the denominators.
Substituting x=0x=0x=0 gives AAA immediately, and x=−1x=-1x=−1 gives BBB.
Both pieces integrate to logarithms; keep the modulus signs, since the arguments change sign across the excluded points.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 1 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: (a) ∫sin⁡2x  dx\displaystyle\int\sin^2 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫sin2xdx, (b) ∫cos⁡3x  dx\displaystyle\int\cos^3 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫cos3xdx, (c) ∫tan⁡2x  dx\displaystyle\int\tan^2 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫tan2xdx.
hints: Classify each integrand first: an even power of sine, an odd power of cosine, and a power of tangent each have their own identity.

In (a) lower the power with sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^2x=\tfrac12(1-\cos2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x). In (b) peel off one cos⁡x\cos xcosx and write cos⁡2x=1−sin⁡2x\cos^2x=1-\sin^2xcos2x=1−sin2x, then substitute u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx.
In (c) use tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1tan2x=sec2x−1; both pieces are then standard. In (a) remember that ∫cos⁡2x dx\int\cos2x\,\mathrm{d}x∫cos2xdx carries a compensating 12\tfrac1221​.

problems.html: ∫ dx9−x2\displaystyle\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}∫9−x2​dx​.
hints: Compare the denominator with the standard form a2−x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}a2−x2​ and read off aaa.
With a=3a=3a=3 the antiderivative is an arcsine of x/ax/ax/a. Differentiate arcsin⁡x3\arcsin\dfrac{x}{3}arcsin3x​ with the chain rule to see exactly what it returns.

The chain rule gives 11−x2/9⋅13=19−x2\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2/9}}\cdot\dfrac13=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}1−x2/9​1​⋅31​=9−x2​1​ — compare that with the integrand before deciding whether any factor is needed out in front.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 3/2 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: Find the area enclosed between y=2xy=2xy=2x and y=x2y=x^2y=x2.
hints: Find where the two curves meet first, by setting 2x=x22x=x^22x=x2 — those points are the limits of integration.
Between them, decide which curve is on top by testing a single intermediate value such as x=1x=1x=1.
The area is the integral of (upper minus lower) across that interval.
problems.format: the enclosed area

problems.html: The region under y=xy=\sqrt{x}y=x​, 0≤x≤40\le x\le 40≤x≤4, is revolved about the xxx-axis. Find the volume.
hints: The disc method gives V=π∫ab[f(x)]2 dxV=\pi\displaystyle\int_a^b [f(x)]^2\,\mathrm{d}xV=π∫ab​[f(x)]2dx — note the square, which is what makes each slice a disc of that radius.
So the integrand is (x)2=x(\sqrt{x})^2=x(x​)2=x, not x\sqrt xx​.
Integrate that between the given limits and multiply by π\piπ.
problems.format: the k in V = kπ

problems.html: Find the average value of f(x)=x2f(x)=x^2f(x)=x2 on [0,3][0,3][0,3].
hints: The average value of fff on [a,b][a,b][a,b] is 1b−a∫abf\dfrac{1}{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^b fb−a1​∫ab​f — the integral divided by the interval's length.
So integrate x2x^2x2 from 000 to 333 first, then divide by 333.
Sanity check: the answer must lie between the smallest and largest values of fff on the interval.
problems.format: the average value

problems.html: The random variable XXX has density f(x)=3x2f(x)=3x^2f(x)=3x2 on [0,1][0,1][0,1] (and 000 elsewhere). Verify it is a density, then find P(X>12)P(X>\tfrac12)P(X>21​) and E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X].
hints: A density needs to be non-negative and to enclose total area exactly 111; check both before going further.
P(X>12)P(X>\tfrac12)P(X>21​) is the area under the density to the right of 12\tfrac1221​, so integrate from 12\tfrac1221​ to 111.

The expectation is E[X]=∫xf(x) dx\mathbb{E}[X]=\int x f(x)\,\mathrm{d}xE[X]=∫xf(x)dx taken over the whole support [0,1][0,1][0,1], not over the event in the previous part — note the extra factor of xxx inside.
problems.format: P(X > ½), then E[X]

problems.html: Evaluate (a) ∫x2ex  dx,(b) ∫arctan⁡x  dx,(c) ∫exsin⁡x  dx.\text{(a) }\int x^2\mathrm{e}^{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) }\int\arctan x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) }\int \mathrm{e}^{x}\sin x\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a) ∫x2exdx,(b) ∫arctanxdx,(c) ∫exsinxdx.
hints: Name the LIATE choice in each part. In (a) the algebraic factor comes before the exponential; in (b) the inverse-trig function stands alone, so pair it with v′=1v'=1v′=1.

In (a) one application leaves ∫2x ex dx\int 2x\,\mathrm{e}^x\,\mathrm{d}x∫2xexdx, which needs parts once more. In (b) the leftover is ∫x1+x2 dx\int\frac{x}{1+x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x∫1+x2x​dx: compare its numerator with the derivative of the denominator.
In (c) neither factor ever simplifies: after two applications the original integral reappears, so call it III and solve for it.
problems.format: (a) at 0, (b) at 1 to 3 d.p., (c) at 0; C=0

problems.html: Evaluate (a) ∫2x+3x(x+1)2  dx,(b) ∫ dxx2+4x+13,(c) ∫x3x2+1  dx.\text{(a) }\int\frac{2x+3}{x(x+1)^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) }\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^2+4x+13},\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) }\int\frac{x^3}{x^2+1}\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a) ∫x(x+1)22x+3​dx,(b) ∫x2+4x+13dx​,(c) ∫x2+1x3​dx.
hints: Look at each denominator first: a linear factor times a repeated one, an irreducible quadratic, and a fraction that is not proper each need a different opening move.

In (a) write Ax+Bx+1+C(x+1)2\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x+1}+\frac{C}{(x+1)^2}xA​+x+1B​+(x+1)2C​. Cover-up gives AAA and CCC but not BBB, so compare the x2x^2x2 coefficients for that. In (b) check the discriminant, then complete the square.
In (c) divide first, since the numerator's degree is not lower than the denominator's. The remainder over x2+1x^2+1x2+1 is then an f′/ff'/ff′/f logarithm.
problems.format: each at x=1 (C=0), to 3 d.p., comma-separated

problems.html: Evaluate (a) ∫0π/2sin⁡3xcos⁡2x  dx,(b) ∫0π/4tan⁡3x  dx,(c) ∫sec⁡4x  dx.\text{(a) }\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^3 x\cos^2 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) }\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^3 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) }\int\sec^4 x\,\,\mathrm{d}x.(a) ∫0π/2​sin3xcos2xdx,(b) ∫0π/4​tan3xdx,(c) ∫sec4xdx.
hints: Classify each integrand: an odd power of sine, an odd power of tangent, an even power of secant. Each has its own identity to reach for.
In (a) peel off one sin⁡x\sin xsinx and substitute u=cos⁡xu=\cos xu=cosx, mapping the limits too. In (b) split off tan⁡2x=sec⁡2x−1\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1tan2x=sec2x−1 and treat the two pieces separately.

In (b) one piece needs ∫tan⁡x dx=ln⁡∣sec⁡x∣\int\tan x\,\mathrm{d}x=\ln|\sec x|∫tanxdx=ln∣secx∣. In (c) save one sec⁡2x\sec^2xsec2x to go with du\mathrm{d}udu for u=tan⁡xu=\tan xu=tanx, and convert the rest with sec⁡2x=1+tan⁡2x\sec^2x=1+\tan^2xsec2x=1+tan2x.
problems.format: (a) exact, (b) to 3 d.p., (c) at π/4 with C=0

problems.html: Evaluate (a) ∫9−x2  dx,(b) ∫ dx(x2+4)3/2.\text{(a) }\int\sqrt{9-x^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b) }\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}.(a) ∫9−x2​dx,(b) ∫(x2+4)3/2dx​.
hints: The shape of the surd tells you the substitution: a2−x2\sqrt{a^2-x^2}a2−x2​ calls for x=asin⁡θx=a\sin\thetax=asinθ, and x2+a2x^2+a^2x2+a2 calls for x=atan⁡θx=a\tan\thetax=atanθ.
In (a) put x=3sin⁡θx=3\sin\thetax=3sinθ; then 9−x2=3cos⁡θ\sqrt{9-x^2}=3\cos\theta9−x2​=3cosθ and dx=3cos⁡θ dθ\mathrm{d}x=3\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\thetadx=3cosθdθ, leaving an even power of cosine.
Convert back to xxx at the end using a right triangle — and remember sin⁡2θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ\sin 2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\thetasin2θ=2sinθcosθ when undoing the double angle.

problems.html:
1. Sketch the region first, then find the area enclosed between the parabola y=x2y=x^2y=x2 and the line y=x+2y=x+2y=x+2.

  2. Find the total area between y=sin⁡xy=\sin xy=sinx and y=cos⁡xy=\cos xy=cosx for 0≤x≤π20\le x\le\tfrac\pi20≤x≤2π​.
hints: Sketch first, then find the intersections — they give the limits, and the sketch tells you which curve is on top.
In (a) solve x2=x+2x^2=x+2x2=x+2 to get the two crossing points, and integrate the difference between them.
In (b) the two curves cross inside the interval, so the top curve changes. Split the integral there and add the magnitudes, since the question asks for total area.
problems.format: (a) exact; then (b) to 3 d.p.

problems.html:
1. Find the volume when the region under y=sin⁡xy=\sin xy=sinx, 0≤x≤π0\le x\le\pi0≤x≤π, is revolved about the xxx-axis.

  2. Revolving y=r2−x2y=\sqrt{r^2-x^2}y=r2−x2​, −r≤x≤r-r\le x\le r−r≤x≤r, about the xxx-axis sweeps out a sphere of radius rrr. The cap of height hhh (0<h≤2r0<h\le2r0<h≤2r) is the part with r−h≤x≤rr-h\le x\le rr−h≤x≤r. Show that its volume is V=13πh2(3r−h)V=\tfrac13\pi h^2(3r-h)V=31​πh2(3r−h), and check that h=2rh=2rh=2r gives the whole sphere.

  3. Spot the error. For the region of Warm-up 1.6 a student writes V=π∫04x  dx=π[23x3/2]04=16π3V=\pi\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\bigl[\tfrac23x^{3/2}\bigr]_0^4=\tfrac{16\pi}{3}V=π∫04​x​dx=π[32​x3/2]04​=316π​, instead of the 8π8\pi8π found there. What went wrong, and what is the correct set-up?
hints: Every part uses the disc method, V=π∫abf(x)2 dxV=\pi\int_a^b f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}xV=π∫ab​f(x)2dx: square the radius before integrating.
In (a) the even power sin⁡2x\sin^2xsin2x needs the half-angle identity. In (b) f(x)2=r2−x2f(x)^2=r^2-x^2f(x)2=r2−x2, integrated from r−hr-hr−h to rrr.
In (b) expand (r−h)3(r-h)^3(r−h)3 carefully and collect powers of hhh; the r3r^3r3 terms cancel. In (c) compare the student's integrand with f(x)2f(x)^2f(x)2.
problems.format: (a) to 3 d.p.; (b) V/π at r=3, h=1; (c) V/π

problems.html: Evaluate, or show divergent: (a) ∫0∞e−2x  dx,(b) ∫0∞x e−x2  dx,(c) ∫1∞ dxxp  (p>0).\text{(a) }\int_0^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-2x}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(b) }\int_0^{\infty}x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\allowbreak \text{(c) }\int_1^{\infty}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x^p}\ \ (p>0).(a) ∫0∞​e−2xdx,(b) ∫0∞​xe−x2dx,(c) ∫1∞​xpdx​  (p>0).
hints: Replace the infinite limit by ttt, integrate over the finite interval, and only then let t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞.
In (b) substitute u=x2u=x^2u=x2 first: the limits 000 and ttt become 000 and t2t^2t2, and the integrand turns into a plain exponential.
In (c) treat p=1p=1p=1 separately, since the antiderivative is a logarithm there. For p≠1p\neq1p=1, ask whether the exponent of ttt in t1−pt^{1-p}t1−p is positive or negative.
problems.format: (a), (b), then the p above which (c) converges

problems.html:
(Exponential law.) The lifetime TTT (hours) of a component has density f(t)=λe−λtf(t)=\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}f(t)=λe−λt on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) with λ=12\lambda=\tfrac12λ=21​.

  1. Find P(T>2)P(T>2)P(T>2).

  2. Find P(1<T<3)P(1<T<3)P(1<T<3).

  3. Find the mean lifetime E[T]\mathbb{E}[T]E[T].
hints: P(T>2)P(T>2)P(T>2) is the area under the density from 222 to infinity, so it is an improper integral.

For an exponential density the antiderivative is easy: ∫λe−λt dt=−e−λt\int\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\,\mathrm{d}t=-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}∫λe−λtdt=−e−λt, so every probability comes out as a difference of exponentials.
For (c) compute E[T]=∫0∞t λe−λt dt\mathbb{E}[T]=\int_0^\infty t\,\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}\,\mathrm{d}tE[T]=∫0∞​tλe−λtdt by parts — the answer is the reciprocal of λ\lambdaλ.
problems.format: (a), (b) to 3 d.p.; then E[T] in hours

problems.html:
A uniform rope of length L=10L=10L=10 m and mass μ=2\mu=2μ=2 kg per metre hangs from a winch at the top of a building. Take g=9.8g=9.8g=9.8 m s−2^{-2}−2.

  1. Find the work done to wind the whole rope to the top.

  2. Find the average depth xˉ\bar xxˉ below the top of the points of the hanging rope, and show that the work in (a) equals the rope’s weight μgL\mu gLμgL times xˉ\bar xxˉ.
hints: Think in slices: a short piece of rope at depth xxx below the top must be lifted through exactly xxx metres.
That piece has weight μg dx\mu g\,\mathrm{d}xμgdx, so it needs work μgx dx\mu g x\,\mathrm{d}xμgxdx; integrate from 000 to LLL.
In (b) the depth xxx is a function on [0,L][0,L][0,L]: its average is its integral divided by the length of the interval. Then compare μgLxˉ\mu gL\bar xμgLxˉ with your WWW.
problems.format: (a) W in joules, (b) x̄ in metres

problems.html:
1. A pyramid of height hhh has as its base an equilateral triangle of side aaa. Measuring xxx down from the apex, use similar triangles to find the area A(x)A(x)A(x) of the cross-section at depth xxx, and show that V=312a2hV=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{12}a^2hV=123​​a2h.

  2. ⋆⋆⋆\star\star\star⋆⋆⋆ challenge A solid has a circular base of radius RRR in the xyxyxy-plane. Every cross-section perpendicular to a fixed diameter is a square. Find its volume.
hints: In (a) the slice at depth xxx is an equilateral triangle similar to the base, so its side scales in proportion to x/hx/hx/h.
An equilateral triangle of side sss has area 34s2\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^243​​s2, so A(x)A(x)A(x) is proportional to x2x^2x2; the volume is ∫0hA(x) dx\int_0^h A(x)\,\mathrm{d}x∫0h​A(x)dx.
In (b) put the fixed diameter along the xxx-axis: the square at xxx has side equal to the chord 2R2−x22\sqrt{R^2-x^2}2R2−x2​. No π\piπ appears, since the slices are squares.
problems.format: (a) A(h/2) ÷ base area; (b) the c in V = cR³

problems.html: ∫2x+3x2+9  dx\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+3}{x^2+9}\,\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2+92x+3​dx.
hints: The denominator is irreducible, so partial fractions will not help — split the numerator instead.
Write 2x+32x+32x+3 as (the derivative of the denominator) plus a constant: the derivative of x2+9x^2+9x2+9 is exactly 2x2x2x.
The first piece is then an f′/ff'/ff′/f logarithm and the second is a standard arctangent with a=3a=3a=3.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 0 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: ∫ dxx2−9\displaystyle\int\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{\sqrt{x^2-9}}∫x2−9​dx​  (for x>3x>3x>3).
hints: The form x2−a2\sqrt{x^2-a^2}x2−a2​ calls for x=asec⁡θx=a\sec\thetax=asecθ — the third of the three trigonometric substitutions.
With a=3a=3a=3, x2−9=3tan⁡θ\sqrt{x^2-9}=3\tan\thetax2−9​=3tanθ and dx=3sec⁡θtan⁡θ dθ\mathrm{d}x=3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\thetadx=3secθtanθdθ; almost everything cancels.
You are left with ∫sec⁡θ dθ=ln⁡∣sec⁡θ+tan⁡θ∣\int\sec\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta=\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|∫secθdθ=ln∣secθ+tanθ∣. Convert back with the triangle, and absorb the constant.
problems.format: the antiderivative at x = 5 (C = 0), to 3 d.p.

problems.html: A particle moves with velocity v(t)=6t−t2v(t)=6t-t^2v(t)=6t−t2 (m s−1^{-1}−1) for 0≤t≤60\le t\le 60≤t≤6. Find its average velocity over this interval.
hints: Average value is the integral divided by the length of the interval.
Here that means 16∫06(6t−t2) dt\frac16\int_0^6(6t-t^2)\,\mathrm{d}t61​∫06​(6t−t2)dt.
Notice what the integral of velocity measures: the total displacement. So the average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time.
problems.format: the average velocity, in m/s

problems.html: Find kkk so that f(x)=kxf(x)=kxf(x)=kx is a probability density on [0,4][0,4][0,4], then compute E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X].
hints: Impose the defining condition of a density: the total area must equal exactly 111.
So set ∫04kx dx=1\int_0^4 kx\,\mathrm{d}x=1∫04​kxdx=1 and solve for kkk; the constant comes outside the integral.
Then compute E[X]=∫04x⋅kx dx\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^4 x\cdot kx\,\mathrm{d}xE[X]=∫04​x⋅kxdx with the kkk you found.
problems.format: k, then E[X]

problems.html:
1. A rod occupies 0≤x≤L0\le x\le L0≤x≤L with linear density ρ(x)=kx\rho(x)=kxρ(x)=kx. Find its mass.

  2. (Physics.) A spring of stiffness 200200200 N m−1^{-1}−1 needs the force F(x)=200xF(x)=200xF(x)=200x to hold it stretched by xxx metres. Find the work done in stretching it from its natural length to x=0.1x=0.1x=0.1 m.
hints: Both parts are slice-and-sum: say what xxx measures, write down the contribution of one slice of width dx\mathrm{d}xdx, and integrate.
In (a) a slice has mass ρ(x) dx=kx dx\rho(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=kx\,\mathrm{d}xρ(x)dx=kxdx. In (b) stretching a further dx\mathrm{d}xdx takes work F(x) dxF(x)\,\mathrm{d}xF(x)dx.
Treat kkk and LLL as constants in (a). In (b) the work is the area of a triangle under the force–extension line, which you can check geometrically.
problems.format: (a) the c in M = ckL², (b) the work in joules

problems.html:
Decide, with a one-line reason, whether each statement is true or false.

  1. Every rational function has an elementary antiderivative (after polynomial division, if needed).

  2. ∫−∞∞x  dx=0\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,\,\mathrm{d}x=0∫−∞∞​xdx=0 because the integrand is odd.

  3. The average value of a continuous fff on [a,b][a,b][a,b] always lies between the minimum and maximum of fff on [a,b][a,b][a,b].
hints: Two are true and one is false. For the false one, a single reason (a divergent half, a counterexample) is enough.
For (a), think about what polynomial division plus partial fractions can always achieve. For (b), ask whether both halves of the improper integral converge on their own.
For (c), squeeze the integral between the constants m(b−a)m(b-a)m(b−a) and M(b−a)M(b-a)M(b−a), where mmm and MMM are the minimum and maximum of fff.
problems.format: (a)–(c): true or false, comma-separated

problems.html: A rod on 0≤x≤L0\le x\le L0≤x≤L has density ρ(x)=ρ0(1+x2L2)\rho(x)=\rho_0\bigl(1+\tfrac{x^2}{L^2}\bigr)ρ(x)=ρ0​(1+L2x2​). Find its mass MMM and the position xˉ=1M∫0Lx ρ(x)  dx\bar x=\dfrac{1}{M}\int_0^L x\,\rho(x)\,\,\mathrm{d}xxˉ=M1​∫0L​xρ(x)dx of its centre of mass.
hints: Mass is ∫0Lρ(x) dx\int_0^L\rho(x)\,\mathrm{d}x∫0L​ρ(x)dx; expand the bracket first so that each term is a simple power.
The x2L2\dfrac{x^2}{L^2}L2x2​ term integrates to L3\dfrac{L}{3}3L​ once the constant is taken outside — treat LLL as a constant throughout.
For the centre of mass, integrate xρ(x)x\rho(x)xρ(x) over the same range and divide by the mass. Check the answer lies between L2\tfrac{L}{2}2L​ and LLL, since the rod is heavier at its far end.
problems.format: the c in M = cρ₀L, then the c in x̄ = cL

problems.html: Given the standard result ∫−∞∞e−x2  dx=π\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}\,\,\mathrm{d}x=\sqrt\pi∫−∞∞​e−x2dx=π​, find the constant ccc making f(x)=c e−x2f(x)=c\,\mathrm{e}^{-x^2}f(x)=ce−x2 a probability density on R\mathbb{R}R, and find E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X].

questions.stem: In ∫x2ln⁡x dx\displaystyle\int x^{2}\ln x\,\mathrm{d}x∫x2lnxdx, which factor should be taken as uuu when integrating by parts?
options: Either — parts works equally well both ways.
ln⁡x\ln xlnx, since differentiating a logarithm simplifies it while integrating one does not.
x2x^{2}x2, since it is the simpler of the two.
Neither; this integral needs a substitution instead.
questions.hint: Ask what each factor becomes when you differentiate it, and which choice leaves you an integral simpler than the one you started with.
questions.why: LIATE ranks Logarithm ahead of Algebraic, and the reason is practical rather than arbitrary. Differentiating ln⁡x\ln xlnx gives 1x\dfrac1xx1​, which cancels a power of the other factor and leaves an elementary integral. Taking u=x2u=x^2u=x2 instead forces you to integrate ln⁡x\ln xlnx first — possible, but it needs its own application of parts and produces a messier integral than the one you started with. The choice does not change the answer, only how much work reaching it costs.

questions.stem: Splitting x(x−1)2\dfrac{x}{(x-1)^{2}}(x−1)2x​ into partial fractions, what form is needed?
options: One term, Ax−1\dfrac{A}{x-1}x−1A​.
Two terms, Ax−1+Bx(x−1)2\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{Bx}{(x-1)^{2}}x−1A​+(x−1)2Bx​.
Two terms, Ax−1+B(x−1)2\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{(x-1)^{2}}x−1A​+(x−1)2B​.
One term, A(x−1)2\dfrac{A}{(x-1)^{2}}(x−1)2A​.
questions.hint: Count the free constants. Can a single one match a general numerator over a squared factor?
questions.why: A repeated linear factor contributes one term for every power up to its multiplicity, so both the first and the second power appear. With a single term there are too few free constants to match a general numerator, and the equations turn out inconsistent. The two pieces then integrate quite differently — the first to a logarithm, the second to a negative power — which is why the split is worth making. Note also that the numerator over a linear factor is always a constant, never a linear expression.

questions.stem: Revolving y=xy=\sqrt{x}y=x​ on [0,4][0,4][0,4] about the xxx-axis, a student writes V=π∫04x dxV=\pi\displaystyle\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{d}xV=π∫04​x​dx. What has gone wrong?
options: The limits should be 000 and 222.
The factor of π\piπ does not belong there.
The integrand must be f(x)2f(x)^{2}f(x)2, so it is xxx, not x\sqrt{x}x​.
Nothing — that is the disc method.
questions.hint: Each slice of the solid is a disc. Write down the *area* of a disc of radius f(x)f(x)f(x).
questions.why: Each slice is a disc of radius f(x)f(x)f(x), and a disc of radius rrr has area πr2\pi r^{2}πr2 — so the integrand is πf(x)2\pi f(x)^{2}πf(x)2, here πx\pi xπx. The student integrated the radius instead of the area, obtaining 16π3\tfrac{16\pi}{3}316π​ where the true volume is 8π8\pi8π. Both the π\piπ and the limits were correct. That same square is what distinguishes the washer formula π∫(Rout2−Rin2)\pi\int\left(R_{\text{out}}^{2}-R_{\text{in}}^{2}\right)π∫(Rout2​−Rin2​) from the difference of the two radii.

options: x=3tan⁡θx=3\tan\thetax=3tanθ
x=3sin⁡θx=3\sin\thetax=3sinθ
u=x2−9u=x^{2}-9u=x2−9

questions.hint: Match the shape of the surd. Which trigonometric identity turns x2−a2x^2-a^2x2−a2 into a perfect square?
questions.why: The three substitutions are matched to three shapes: a2−x2\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}a2−x2​ takes asin⁡θa\sin\thetaasinθ, a2+x2\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}a2+x2​ takes atan⁡θa\tan\thetaatanθ, and x2−a2\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}x2−a2​ takes asec⁡θa\sec\thetaasecθ. Here the surd has x2x^{2}x2 first, so the secant is the one that makes it collapse: 9sec⁡2θ−9=3tan⁡θ\sqrt{9\sec^{2}\theta-9}=3\tan\theta9sec2θ−9​=3tanθ. A sine substitution would put a negative quantity under the root, and the plain substitution u=x2−9u=x^{2}-9u=x2−9 fails because there is no spare factor of xxx to supply the du\mathrm{d}udu.

questions.stem: What is the value of ∫−11dxx2\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}}∫−11​x2dx​?
options: 222, twice the integral from 000 to 111.
It diverges: the integrand blows up at x=0x=0x=0, which lies inside the interval.
−2-2−2, by the fundamental theorem.
000, since the integrand is even.
questions.hint: Look at the integrand at x=0x=0x=0 before reaching for an antiderivative.
questions.why: The integrand is unbounded at the origin, so despite its finite-looking limits this is an improper integral: split it there and treat each half as a limit. Each half gives ∫ε1dxx2=1ε−1→∞\int_{\varepsilon}^{1}\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{x^{2}}=\dfrac1\varepsilon-1\to\infty∫ε1​x2dx​=ε1​−1→∞, so both diverge and so does the whole. Applying the fundamental theorem blindly returns −2-2−2, impossible for a positive integrand — the tell-tale that its continuity hypothesis was violated. The integrand is indeed even, but that is irrelevant once the integral fails to exist.

questions.stem: Must the average value of a continuous fff on [a,b][a,b][a,b] lie between the minimum and maximum of fff there?
options: Only if fff is monotonic on the interval.
Yes: the integral is squeezed between m(b−a)m(b-a)m(b−a) and M(b−a)M(b-a)M(b−a).
Only if fff is non-negative on the interval.
No — it can exceed the maximum when fff changes rapidly.
questions.hint: Start from m≤f(x)≤Mm\le f(x)\le Mm≤f(x)≤M and integrate all three parts over [a,b][a,b][a,b].
questions.why: If m≤f(x)≤Mm\le f(x)\le Mm≤f(x)≤M throughout, integrating preserves the inequality, giving m(b−a)≤∫abf≤M(b−a)m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f\le M(b-a)m(b−a)≤∫ab​f≤M(b−a); dividing by b−ab-ab−a places the average between mmm and MMM. Neither the sign of fff nor its monotonicity enters the argument — only continuity, which by the extreme value theorem of Unit 8 also guarantees that mmm and MMM are actually attained. The mean value theorem for integrals says more still: the average is a value fff itself takes somewhere inside the interval.

questions.stem: What is ∫sin⁡2x dx\displaystyle\int\sin^{2}x\,\mathrm{d}x∫sin2xdx?
options: 13sin⁡3x+C\tfrac13\sin^{3}x+C31​sin3x+C, by the power rule.
x2−sin⁡2x4+C\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\sin 2x}{4}+C2x​−4sin2x​+C, after using sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^{2}x=\tfrac12\left(1-\cos2x\right)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x).
12sin⁡2x+C\tfrac12\sin^{2}x+C21​sin2x+C
−13cos⁡3x+C-\tfrac13\cos^{3}x+C−31​cos3x+C
questions.hint: There is no inside function with its derivative sitting beside it, so substitution has nothing to bite on. Which identity removes the power altogether?
questions.why: The power rule is about xnx^{n}xn, not about a power of a function: differentiating 13sin⁡3x\tfrac13\sin^{3}x31​sin3x gives sin⁡2xcos⁡x\sin^{2}x\cos xsin2xcosx, which carries a stray cos⁡x\cos xcosx. An even power of sine offers no spare factor to absorb into du\mathrm{d}udu, so substitution is not available and the way in is the half-angle identity sin⁡2x=12(1−cos⁡2x)\sin^{2}x=\tfrac12(1-\cos2x)sin2x=21​(1−cos2x), which integrates term by term to x2−sin⁡2x4+C\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\sin2x}{4}+C2x​−4sin2x​+C. Differentiating back gives 12−12cos⁡2x=sin⁡2x\tfrac12-\tfrac12\cos2x=\sin^{2}x21​−21​cos2x=sin2x, which is the check worth doing. The odd-power case is genuinely different: ∫sin⁡2xcos⁡x dx\int\sin^{2}x\cos x\,\mathrm{d}x∫sin2xcosxdx does yield to u=sin⁡xu=\sin xu=sinx, because the lone cos⁡x\cos xcosx is exactly du\mathrm{d}udu.

questions.stem: XXX has the exponential density f(x)=λe−λxf(x)=\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}f(x)=λe−λx for x≥0x\ge0x≥0. What is E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X]?
options: λ\lambdaλ
1λ\dfrac{1}{\lambda}λ1​
1λ2\dfrac{1}{\lambda^{2}}λ21​
111, since the density integrates to 111.
questions.hint: The mean is the integral of xxx weighted by the density. Set it up, and integrate by parts with u=xu=xu=x.
questions.why: By definition E[X]=∫0∞x λe−λx dx\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{0}^{\infty}x\,\lambda\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda x}\,\mathrm{d}xE[X]=∫0∞​xλe−λxdx, and integrating by parts with u=xu=xu=x gives 1λ\tfrac1\lambdaλ1​. The trap is option 333: ∫f=1\int f=1∫f=1 is the normalisation, true of every density whatever its shape, so it can never be the mean — it is what makes fff a density in the first place. There is a sanity check that settles the answer without any integration: a larger λ\lambdaλ means faster decay, hence a distribution packed closer to 000 and a smaller mean, so the mean must fall as λ\lambdaλ rises. That rules out λ\lambdaλ itself. And 1λ2\tfrac{1}{\lambda^{2}}λ21​ is the variance.

questions.stem: On an interval where fff is concave up, how does the trapezium rule compare with the true integral?
options: It is exact.
It may do either, depending on the sign of fff.
It overestimates it.
It underestimates it.
questions.hint: Draw a single strip. When the curve bends upwards, where does the straight chord joining the endpoints sit relative to it?
questions.why: On a concave-up arc the chord joining the two endpoints lies above the curve, so every trapezium contains its true strip and the total comes out too large. Concave down reverses the argument and the rule underestimates. The rule is exact only where fff is linear on each strip, chord and curve then coinciding. The sign of fff is irrelevant: the argument is about which way the curve bends, not how high it sits, and shifting fff upwards adds the same rectangle to both the estimate and the truth. Simpson's rule fits a parabola through three points instead of a chord through two, which is why it does so much better — it is exact for cubics.
